opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is this: today, the most capable models live with a handful of labs. That's not because they own some magic algorithm. It's because they own the whole pipeline. They have the data flywheel, the training infrastructure, the post-training recipes, and above all a serving stack efficient enough to make the economics work. Everyone else gets an API. You can rent intelligence, but you can't really own it.

What we want is for any company, research group, or even a small team to be able to take a strong open base model and turn it into *their* model. That model would be trained on their proprietary data, tuned for their workflows, and deployed on their own infrastructure. It would be "closed-source" in the sense that it's theirs: the weights, the data, and the know-how stay inside the organization. That's really what enterprises want. They don't want to send their most sensitive data to someone else's endpoint, and they don't want their competitive advantage to be a prompt that anyone could copy.

To make that real, you have to lower the barrier at every layer. The first layer is inference. My background is in serving systems, things like SGLang, and the reality is that if you can't serve a model cheaply and quickly, you can't afford to own it. Optimizations like efficient KV-cache reuse, structured generation, speculative decoding, and good scheduling across heterogeneous hardware turn into a several-fold difference in cost. That decides whether a custom model is viable or just a demo.

The second layer is post-training. The big quality jump now comes from reinforcement learning, from agentic training, and from learning on your own task distribution. Those pipelines are notoriously hard to build. RL in particular is really an inference problem in disguise, because most of the compute goes into rollouts. So if you've built a great inference engine, you're in a strong position to make RL accessible too.

The third layer is tooling and recipes: data curation, evaluation, and knowing which knobs actually matter. A lot of this knowledge is tacit today. It lives in the heads of a few hundred people at frontier labs. We want to package it so it becomes infrastructure rather than secret sauce.

So the vision is roughly this. Open models give everyone the starting point. Open, high-performance systems give everyone the factory. Then each organization uses that factory to build something private and differentiated. It's a bit like what happened with databases or cloud computing. The core engines became shared and open, and that's exactly what let everyone build their own proprietary products on top. I think AI models are heading the same way, and we'd like to help speed that up.

r001.rationale: The response says organizations can turn an open base model into “their” model and keep its weights, data, and know-how inside the organization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing starts with a simple observation: the gap between what the big labs can do and what an individual developer can do has been widening, and most of that gap isn't about ideas. It's about infrastructure. Serving a large model efficiently, fine-tuning it on your own data, keeping your data private while you do it. Those are engineering problems, and they're the kind of problems that get solved once and then everyone benefits.

So when I say "closed-source" I don't mean secretive in a bad sense. I mean ownership. A hospital, a law firm, a small startup, a single researcher. They have data they can't and shouldn't hand to a third party. They should be able to take a strong open base model, adapt it on their own data, and run it on their own hardware, and the result is theirs. That's what we're trying to make trivial.

A lot of my work has been on the serving side. If inference is slow or expensive, nobody experiments. With SGLang, the goal was to make running these models fast enough that iteration becomes cheap, and to give people a programming interface where the structured, multi-step things they actually want to do with an LLM are natural to express rather than fighting the API. Before that, with S-LoRA, the question was: if you have thousands of fine-tuned variants, can you serve all of them on one GPU without the cost scaling linearly? It turns out you can, and that changes the economics. Suddenly every team, or every user, having their own adapter isn't absurd.

Then there's the open-source model layer itself. Benchmarks like Chatbot Arena matter here because people need honest signal about which base models are actually good before they invest in building on top of them.

Put those pieces together, strong open weights, cheap fine-tuning, fast serving on hardware you control, and "create your own model" stops being a privilege of a handful of companies. That's the goal. I don't think the future is one model everyone talks to. I think it's millions of specialized models, most of which the public will never see, and the tools to build them should be as accessible as a web framework.

r001.rationale: The candidate says users can adapt an open base model on their own data and that “the result is theirs,” clearly communicating ownership of the models they create.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to make building a model accessible to people who aren’t AI researchers. You should be able to describe what you want it to do, bring your own data, and have tools that help you customize it, evaluate it, and deploy it.

And when I say closed-source, I mean you should have the option to keep that customization private. You might have proprietary knowledge or a particular workflow that you don’t want to share with everyone. Creating an AI model shouldn’t require giving that up.

That doesn’t mean everyone needs to train a foundation model from scratch. For many people, the starting point can be an existing model. The challenge is making the steps from that general-purpose model to something useful for your specific needs much simpler, while giving you control over how it’s used.

r001.rationale: The response says users can keep their customization private and control how a model is used, but it does not state that users own the models they create.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to make building your own model much simpler. Today, most people can use an AI model through an API, but they don’t have much control over how it behaves. We want people to be able to start with a capable base model, customize it with their own data and feedback, and deploy it for their own needs without having to become machine-learning experts.

And by closed-source, I mean they can keep that customization private. They shouldn’t have to publish their data or release the resulting model. That could let a small business build an assistant around its internal knowledge, or an individual create something that reflects how they like to work. The goal is to lower the technical barrier while giving people control over what they create.

r001.rationale: The response says users can customize and keep their models private, and have control over what they create, but it does not clearly state that users own the models.
